summary.text: The Chinese remainder theorem says that if you know the remainders of a whole number after division by several numbers with no shared factors, you can determine its remainder after division by their product.
For example, remainders of 2, 3 and 2 when dividing by 3, 5 and 7 give 23 as the only possible positive value below 105.
It is widely used for computing with large integers, replacing one big computation with several similar ones on small integers.

facts.label: Classic puzzle
facts.value: Count by threes: 2 left; by fives: 3 left; by sevens: 2 left

facts.label: Worked answer
facts.value: Remainders 2, 3 and 2 point to 23, the only value below 105

facts.label: Early algorithm
facts.value: Aryabhata described one in the 6th century

facts.label: Full solution
facts.value: Qin Jiushao gave a complete one in 1247, called Da-yan-shu

facts.label: Modern use
facts.value: Called multi-modular computation for integer linear algebra

items.prompt: A bag of coins leaves 2 over in groups of 3, 3 over in groups of 5, and 2 over in groups of 7. How many different counts below 105 fit all three clues?

options.label: One for each clue, so three
Exactly one
Every count below 105
None, since the clues clash

items.explain: With the divisors 3, 5 and 7, the remainders fix a single value below 105, which is 23.

items.prompt: A teacher gives remainders for divisors 4 and 6 and expects a single answer for the product. Why might this fail?

options.label: Divisors must be even for the theorem to apply
Remainders must all be zero
4 and 6 share a common factor other than 1
Only three divisors at a time are allowed

items.explain: The theorem needs the divisors to be pairwise coprime: no two may share a common factor other than 1. 4 and 6 share 2.

items.prompt: Two numbers leave the same remainders when divided by 3, 5 and 7. What must be true of their difference?

options.label: It is divisible by 105
It is exactly 105
It is divisible only by 3
It must be a prime number

items.explain: The difference is a multiple of each divisor. Because they are pairwise coprime, their product, 105, also divides it.

items.prompt: Why is the theorem helpful when a computer must handle huge integers?

options.label: It makes every large number turn out to be a prime
It swaps one big sum for several small-number sums
It rounds any large number down to exactly zero
It removes any need for remainders in the working

items.explain: When a bound on the result's size is known, the work can be split into several computations on small integers.

items.prompt: Carl Friedrich Gauss illustrated the theorem with a problem about what?

options.label: Weighing coins on a balance
Folding paper into equal parts
Calendars: years in the solar and lunar cycles
Counting the stars in a constellation

items.explain: Gauss used a problem about finding years with a certain period number in the solar and lunar cycle and the Roman indiction.

items.prompt: Why would Sunzi's counting puzzle not be called a theorem by modern standards?

options.label: It uses only numbers that are below 10 in size
Its answer was later found to be wrong
It was written down much too recently
It gives one problem, with no general method or proof

items.explain: It states a single problem without showing how to solve it, and with no proof or algorithm for the general case.
